source_text:
THE UNOPENED LETTER
A short family drama in four scenes.

Written for cultural adaptation (source is culturally neutral).


SCENE 1
EXT. HOUSE FRONT YARD - EARLY MORNING

A modest two-storey house. Dew on the grass. A metal gate that never quite closes. ADAM (28), restless, stands with an unopened envelope. He has not slept.

MOTHER (55) watches from the doorway, a shawl around her shoulders. SISTER (22) sits on the low wall, pretending to check her phone.

                    MOTHER
          You came back late. You always do this
          when something is wrong.

                    ADAM
          Nothing is wrong. I just needed air.

He turns the envelope over. The handwriting is his uncle's.

                    SISTER
          That letter has been in your pocket for
          two days. Either open it or give it to her.

                    MOTHER
          If it is from my brother, it is a family
          matter. Do not hide family matters from me.

Adam does not answer. He puts the letter back in his jacket pocket and walks toward the kitchen door. Mother's worry stays on her face. Sister follows him with her eyes, then looks down.


SCENE 2
INT. KITCHEN - MORNING

Steam from a kettle. Three cups wait on the table. The kitchen is the true centre of the house. FRIEND (27) has arrived early, as he always does when Adam is in trouble. He leans against the counter, trying to keep the mood light.

                    FRIEND
          You look like a man who lost a bet and
          then lost the walk home.

                    ADAM
          My uncle wrote. He wants me to take the
          shop. Mother still thinks I am studying.

                    SISTER
          You told her you had one year left.

                    MOTHER
          I can hear you. I am not a guest in my
          own kitchen.

Silence. Adam's hand stays on the pocket that holds the letter. The kettle clicks off.

                    MOTHER
          Sit. Drink. Then tell me the truth, not
          the version you prepared for strangers.

Adam sits. He does not take the letter out. Sister places a cup in front of him, then one in front of Mother. Friend looks at the floor, suddenly not funny.

                    ADAM
          After work. I will tell you after work.

                    MOTHER
          After work is how lies grow old.

Adam stands, still carrying the letter, and leaves through the back door. Sister starts to speak, then stops.


SCENE 3
EXT. MARKET STREET - AFTERNOON

A busy street of small shops, buses, and heat. Adam walks with Friend. The letter is still in his pocket. A hawker calls out. A bicycle bell cuts through the noise.

                    FRIEND
          If you take the shop, you stay. If you
          stay, you become the man she already
          introduced to the neighbours.

                    ADAM
          If I refuse, she will think I am ashamed
          of her brother's work.

                    FRIEND
          Then do not refuse in the street. Go home
          and let her see your face when you say it.

They stop near a tea stall. Adam almost opens the envelope, then puts it away again.

                    FRIEND
          Your sister already knows. Your mother
          almost knows. The only person still
          pretending is you.

                    ADAM
          I will go home before evening. I will not
          bring a stranger's courage with me.

He keeps the letter. They part. The market continues without noticing.


SCENE 4
INT. LIVING ROOM - EVENING

The house is quieter. A single lamp. Mother sits in the main chair. Sister stands near the window. Adam enters, dusty from the street, the same jacket, the same letter.

He takes the envelope out and places it on the low table between them. He does not sit until Mother nods.

                    ADAM
          Uncle asked me to leave the course and
          take the shop. I hid the letter because
          I was afraid of disappointing you.

                    MOTHER
          I can survive disappointment. I cannot
          survive being the last to know.

                    SISTER
          We would have sat with you. That is the
          whole point of this house.

                    ADAM
          I am sorry. I am still not sure I want
          the shop. I am sure I should have said so.

Mother picks up the letter, feels its weight, and does not open it yet. She looks at her son, then at her daughter.

                    MOTHER
          Then we will read it together. After that,
          you will tell me what you want, not what
          you think I can bear.

Sister sits. Adam sits. The letter stays on the table, no longer hidden, not yet finished.

END.

adaptation_plan.summary: Adapt the letter drama into Majhi Punjabi (rural Majha — Amritsar / Tarn Taran belt, Punjab). Household spaces (aangan, rasoi, baithak) remain the moral engine. Dialect is never the joke.

decisions.adapted: Mother→Surjit Kaur, Adam→Jaswant Singh, Uncle→Mama Jagtar Singh, Sister→Simran Kaur, Friend→Harpreet Singh
decisions.reason: Majhi kinship and village izzat need specific names, not generic North Indian labels.

decisions.source: an unnamed shop and a course
decisions.adapted: Mama Jagtar's kiryana on the pind chowk versus Jaswant's remaining college year
decisions.reason: The conflict is izzat and mother's brother's trust, not a generic career plot.

decisions.adapted: Majhi-Roman (and optional Gurmukhi) with Bebe, puttar, chiTThi, rasoi, baithak
decisions.reason: Kinship and household space carry the drama; vocabulary-only translation would fail.

decisions.source: standing in a yard, sitting in a kitchen
decisions.adapted: Bebe in the doorway with covered head; no one takes her baithak chair until she nods; letter placed on the low table, not handed in the street
decisions.reason: Do not sit in Bebe's chair until she nods; cover the head in the baithak when the matter is serious

decisions.adapted: rural Majha kothi and mandi road
decisions.reason: Exact Majha architecture, phulkari-border dupatta, kara, juttis, steel glasses.

decisions.adapted: Yaar teasing about a lost shart, never mocking the dialect itself
decisions.reason: Dry teasing (yaar, lost a bet) rather than slapstick; never use dialect as the joke

decisions.adapted: Same arc. Public refusal is culturally worse, so Scene 3 pushes him home rather than changing his goal.
decisions.reason: Cultural change must not reverse Adam's motivation.

uncertain_choices: Exact neighbourhood slang varies between Amritsar city and village Majha; rural register is used unless the user selects urban.
Kinship tone after conflict is contested in some families; Bebe remains the default maternal address.

SCENE 1
EXT. KOTHI DA AANGAN - EARLY MORNING

Brick kothi with a small aangan, iron gate that never latches, peepal shade at the wall, charpai against the verandah

A modest do-manzila kothi. Dew on the grass. A lohe da gate that never quite closes. Jaswant (28), restless, stands with an unopened envelope. He has not slept.
Bebe (55) watches from the verandah de darwaze, a phulkari-border dupatta around her shoulders. Simran (22) sits on the aangan di kandh, pretending to check her mobile.
He turns the envelope over. The handwriting is his Mama's.
Jaswant does not answer. He puts the letter back in his khaddar jacket de pocket and walks toward the rasoi door. Bebe's worry stays on her face. Simran follows him with her eyes, then looks down.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Tu late aa gya, puttar. Jadon kujh gal hundi ae, tu
          aidaan hi ghumda ae.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Kujh gal nahi, Bebe. Saah lain nu bahar aaya si.

                    SIMRAN KAUR
          Oh chiTThi do din to pocket vich pae. Ja khol, ja
          Bebe nu de de.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Je mere veer di chiTThi ae te eh ghar di gal ae.
          Ghar di gal merethon lukai nahi jaandi.


SCENE 2
INT. RASOI - MORNING

Smoke-darkened rasoi with a gas stove, steel glasses, aluminium kettle, and a wooden almirah of masala tins

Steam from a aluminium kettle. Three steel glasses wait on the table. The rasoi is the true centre of the house. Harpreet (27) has arrived early, as he always does when Jaswant is in trouble. He leans against the counter, trying to keep the mood light.
Silence. Jaswant's hand stays on the pocket that holds the letter. The aluminium kettle clicks off.
Jaswant sits. He does not take the letter out. Simran places a cup in front of him, then one in front of Bebe. Harpreet looks at the floor, suddenly not funny.
Jaswant stands, still carrying the letter, and leaves through the back door. Simran starts to speak, then stops.

                    HARPREET SINGH
          Aidaan lagda ae jaan shart haar ke rasta vi haar
          aaya hovein, yaar.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Mama Jagtar ne likheya ae. Ohnu shop chahidi ae mere
          kolon. Bebe hun vi samajhdi ae main padhda peaa
          haan.

                    SIMRAN KAUR
          Tainu ohnau dassiya si ikk saal baaki ae.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Main sunn rahi haan. Apni rasoi vich main koi parai
          nahi.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Beh ja. Chai pee le. Phir sach dass, oh gal nahi jo
          tu bazaar vaaste tyaar karke rakhi ae.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Kam ton baad, Bebe. Main dasanga kam ton baad.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Kam ton baad di gal naal jhooth buddha ho janda ae.


SCENE 3
EXT. PIND DA CHOWK / MANDI ROAD - AFTERNOON

Open mandi road with kiryana, cycle-repair, and a reri of kulche-chole; buses throw dust

A busy street of small shops, buses, and heat. Jaswant walks with Harpreet. The letter is still in his pocket. A hawker calls out. A bicycle bell cuts through the noise.
They stop near a kulche-chole di reri. Jaswant almost opens the envelope, then puts it away again.
He keeps the letter. They part. The pind da chowk continues without noticing.

                    HARPREET SINGH
          Je shop le li, tu pind vich rehna. Te je rehana, oh
          bande banjna jehda Bebe ne paise nu pehlan hi dass
          chhaddiya ae.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Je na kar ditta, Bebe kahegi main Mama de kam ton
          sharmaunda haan.

                    HARPREET SINGH
          Phir gall gali vich na kar. Ghar ja, Bebe tere moonh
          te vece je tu gall karein.

                    HARPREET SINGH
          Simran jaandi ae. Bebe lagbhag jaandi ae. Naatak
          sirf tu karan peaa ae.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Shaam ton pehlan ghar jaanga. Kise paraye di himmat
          chukk ke nahi avanga.


SCENE 4
INT. BAITHAK - EVENING

Baithak with one sofa, floor dari, framed family photograph, and a low table for the letter

The house is quieter. A single lamp. Bebe sits in the Bebe di kursi. Simran stands near the window. Jaswant enters, dusty from the street, the same khaddar jacket, the same letter.
He takes the envelope out and places it on the chhoti mez between them. He does not sit until Bebe nods. He waits for Bebe's nod before taking a seat — baithak etiquette.
Bebe picks up the letter, feels its weight, and does not open it yet. She looks at her son, then at her daughter.
Simran sits. Jaswant sits. The letter stays on the table, no longer hidden, not yet finished.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Mama ne course chhadd ke kiryana sambhalan nu keha
          ae. ChiTThi is vaaste lukai kyunki mainu darr si
          tuhanu niiraan na kar deaan.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Niiraan te main seh laini aan, puttar. Par ghar vich
          aakhri jaanan vaali nahi ban sakdi.

                    SIMRAN KAUR
          Assi tere naal behnde. Eh kothi da matlab hi eh ae.

                    JASWANT SINGH
          Maaf kar de, Bebe. Shop baare hun vi pakka nahi.
          Pakka eh ae ke pehlan dassna chahida si.

                    SURJIT KAUR
          Phir assaN ikkThhe paRhange. Us ton baad tu oh dass
          jehda tainu chahida ae, oh nahi jehda tainu lagda ae
          main seh sakdi haan.


END.
